newsitem.title: FRANCE: Unions persevere with French rail reform protest.
newsitem.headline: Unions persevere with French rail reform protest.

text.p: France's two largest railway unions are persevering with a protest against government plans to split the SNCF state rail company after a moderately successful strike on Thursday, but finding it hard to mobilise their troops.

One in three SNCF staff joined the strike called by the CGT and CFDT unions, causing considerable disruption, but less than the strikes of 1995, when a far more immediate threat of losing early retirement rights made it easier to mobilise rail staff.

Bruno Dalberto, leader of of the Socialist CFDT union's rail federation, said on Friday that there was no question over his members' opposition to the plans to set up a new company which would own the rail network and charge the SNCF for using it.

He said a successful campaign by the government and the SNCF management had masked a serious threat to pay and work conditions as the SNCF started paying to use the rail network, on top of a cost-cutting drive.
"It will be paying six billion francs this year and next and in 1999 it will be revised upwards," Dalberto told Reuters.
This, on top of an agreement between SNCF head Louis Gallois and Prime Minister Alain Juppe to drive operating costs down, would increase the pressure on wages and conditions, he said.

The Communist-led CGT, which represents more than 40 percent of rail workers, has called in the wake of Thursday's strike for follow-up action on February 5, but has not issued strike notice at national level.

It has called for "a day of multiple actions" and issued strike notice at local level, a move which would cover any kind of local protest but falls well short of demanding a nationwide, fullscale strike.
The CFDT has also scaled back its ambitions from Thursday and has opted for a protest rally outside the parliamentary National Assembly in Paris on the same day.

"It's extremely difficult to make this (issue) visible and comprehensible to all, and public opinion doesn't understand it well either," Dalberto said. "But that does not mean that the reform is accepted, quite the contrary," he added.
"We're looking to keep disruption to a minimum" on February 5, he said, adding that school holidays started the same day.
Dalberto said there was a risk of some limited rail disruption in towns such as Marseille in the south, where turnout for the strike on Thursday was a hefty 67 percent.

Transport Minister Bernard Pons says there is no threat in the reform and that the new state company which would own the network would relieve the SNCF of 134 billion francs in debt, out of total debt of 208 billion francs.
He has the backing of unions representing a minority of SNCF staff.
But Dalberto dismisses this as a pure accounting exercise and said that the SNCF would end up footing the bill through the toll fees. "Instead of having one hole, there'll be two," he said.
Both the CGT and CFDT also believes splitting the SNCF in this way opens the way to ending the rail monopoly.
